title: How to make the most of your KOLs at congresses worldwide
overview: Major congresses bring the world's leading interventionalists into one building. Here's how to capture KOL content there, on the booth and in a studio nearby, from opportunistic interviews to planned case presentations and live production.
author: Made Clear
body:
For four or five days a year, the people you most want on camera are all in the same building. The interventional cardiologists who run the trials, chair the sessions and shape how their peers treat patients fly in from Europe, the US, Asia and Latin America for EuroPCR, TCT, ACC, ESC and SCAI. For the rest of the year they're spread across a dozen time zones, in clinics, cath labs and operating theatres, with diaries that are full months ahead.

That makes a major congress the richest content environment in medtech. Yet many companies treat it only as a place to show up: build the booth, run the symposium, fly home. The ones who get the most from it plan for content capture as carefully as they plan the stand.

Over the years we've filmed with key opinion leaders (KOLs) at EuroPCR, TCT, ACC, ESC, SCAI and CIRSE, on the booth, around the congress and in studios set up close by. Here's what we've learned about making the most of them.

Why congresses work for KOL content

Access. Getting a world-leading interventionalist into a studio for an afternoon normally means weeks of back and forth, travel, and fitting around a clinical schedule. At a congress they're already there, and often between sessions with an hour to spare. A KOL who would never travel for a single interview will happily give you twenty minutes on the stand or walk five minutes to a studio.

A global network in one place. A congress lets you bring together voices you couldn't otherwise put side by side: a European operator and a US operator discussing the same case, or a faculty drawn from four countries for a single programme. For live production, such as a broadcast, a case discussion or a panel, that's an opportunity that's hard to recreate at any other time of year.

Cost. The crew, kit and travel are spread across days of filming and dozens of contributors. The cost per finished piece of content falls sharply compared with filming each KOL separately, in their own city, on their own schedule.

Energy. Physicians at a congress are in the middle of the conversation. They've just come out of a late-breaking trial session or a live case, and they have something to say about it. That immediacy comes across on camera in a way a studio interview months later rarely matches.

Two ways to capture: opportunistic and strategic

The best congress content plans combine both.

Opportunistic capture is about being ready. A filming set on the booth, a crew with handheld kit moving through the hall, a photographer covering sessions and the stand. When a KOL drops by, a presentation draws a crowd or a physician has a strong reaction to a new device, you get it. At TCT 2026 we ran an always-on filming booth on Shockwave Medical's stand, recording single and two-person interviews with KOLs, physicians and the leadership team throughout the congress, alongside short social content filmed with physicians on the day.

Strategic capture is planned well before the congress opens. You know which KOLs you need, what each one should talk about and how the footage will be used afterwards. Interviews are scheduled around the session timetable, questions are agreed in advance, and the content is designed to fill specific gaps in a campaign or education programme. Case presentations, where a KOL walks through a real patient case, imaging and all, need this level of preparation.

The two support each other. A planned schedule gives the week its backbone; the opportunistic coverage catches everything the schedule couldn't predict.

On the booth

A filming set on the stand turns the booth into a reason to visit. Physicians who stop for an interview stay to see the device, and the activity draws attention from the aisle. Booth filming suits short, punchy content: reactions, quick takes on new data, short testimonials and social clips that can go out while the congress is still running.

It needs care. A congress hall is loud, busy and badly lit for filming, so sound, lighting and framing have to be planned around the stand design, not added at the last minute. At CIRSE 2026, our crew filmed KOLs and ran VR on Shockwave Medical's stand side by side, so the booth worked as both a demo space and a content studio.

In a studio close to the congress

Some content needs a quieter room. Longer interviews, detailed case presentations, panel discussions and live broadcasts work best in a studio within a short walk of the congress centre, where you control sound, light and time. KOLs can slip out between sessions and be back for the next one, and you get footage that holds up for long-form education and documentary.

This is also where live production comes into its own. With a global faculty already in town, a studio near the congress can host a live case discussion or broadcast that would otherwise mean flying everyone in. We've produced education programmes this way, from The Calcium Masterclass, a peer-to-peer programme taught by a world-class faculty from Europe and the US live from a London studio, to live coverage of pivotal trial results at ACC for Medtronic's HTN:RDN campaign.

Beyond the device: events around the congress

Congresses aren't only about product. At Women As One's RISE 2026, alongside the ESC Congress in Munich, we ran a headshot booth, street interviews and a walk-up Q&A, and turned the day into highlight films for social. Satellite events, society meetings and evening launches gather the same global network, and they're often more relaxed settings for interviews than the congress floor. At EuroPCR 2026 we covered the booth, hands-on training, symposia, KOL portraits and an offsite launch evening across three days.

Making it count

  • Start early. KOL diaries fill up weeks before the congress. Lock in interview slots with your medical affairs and marketing teams as soon as the faculty is known.
  • Know what each piece is for. Plan the outputs first (education modules, campaign films, social clips, sales tools), then work back to the questions and the contributors.
  • Recce the venue. Walk the hall, the stand and the studio before day one, so the crew knows where to film, where the noise is and how long it takes a KOL to get from a session room to the set.
  • Brief the stand team. The people on the booth are your best spotters. If they know who you want to film, they can bring KOLs over.
  • Turn content around quickly. Social clips and highlights edited on site keep your presence going while the congress is still the talk of the field.
  • Keep the footage working. A good congress shoot feeds content for months: education, campaigns, field sales and the next congress.

The KOLs your audience trusts most will all be in one place at the next major congress. With a plan, the right crew and a studio nearby, that week can give you a year's worth of content.
